facts.claim: "Bow Down" is a 2:03 track by SPINALL featuring Amaarae. It is track 9 on his album TOP BOY, released 17 February 2023.
The song was released by TheCAPMusic as part of the album Top Boy.
Songwriting credits go to Ama Serwah Genfi (Amaarae) and Sodamola Oluseye Desmond (Spinall).
Spinall is the sole credited producer of "Bow Down". He is also credited as main artist, mixing engineer, mastering engineer and writer on the album.
Top Boy is Spinall's sixth studio album. The Wikipedia album page gives its recording period as 2021–2023.
Spinall told Apple Music's Dadaboy Ehiz that the album title was inspired by people who "have beaten the odds" and used the resources available to them to succeed.
African Folder says the song shows Spinall's allegiance to the alté movement, through his enlisting of Ghanaian singer Amaarae.
iMullar's review praises Amaarae's performance on "Bow Down". It highlights trumpet horns in the production and a flowing second verse, and calls it one of the album's stand-out performances.
Afrocritik called "Bow Down" a slightly disappointing effort. It said the sparse instrumentals did not quite match Amaarae's sound.
Spinall is a Nigerian DJ and producer who brands his style TheCAP (The CrazyAzzParty). He is sometimes known as Top Boy and began as a radio DJ.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Nigerian DJ-led, genre-crossing Afrobeats and amapiano album tradition, with Ghanaian alté vocalist Amaarae as the guest.

draft:
The hook of **Bow Down** sounds like a command until you hear how it ends. "Bow down, baby bow" repeats like an order, and then it turns into a request: "Make me bow down / To it please." The song is about holding power and wanting to give it up, and it never decides between the two. That is why it works.

Amaarae, the Ghanaian singer SPINALL brought in for this track, spends the first verse in full possession. There's money in the pocket. There's a demand for naira, cedi and dollars, the currencies of Lagos, Accra and everywhere else, a small map of the partnership itself. Prayer shows up early, but only to ask for more. Then the narrator claims divinity outright, the holy spirit arriving among the godless. By the refrain, someone is being worshipped: "Feels like Gods giving praise to me." Sacred language is everywhere, and all of it is spent on appetite.

The second verse loosens things. It's playful and flirty, with a Bee Gees joke and Fiji water, and it says plainly that this won't be kept PG. The confession comes in the lines about being lost in the sauce and lost in thought. Both admit that the one in charge is also the one carried away. Pride and surrender sit in the same breath, and the song lets you feel both without asking you to pick one.

SPINALL, the Nigerian DJ who began on radio and calls his style TheCAP, produced, mixed and mastered it himself. He wrote it with Amaarae for his sixth album, *TOP BOY*, which he said was named for people who beat the odds with whatever they had. The beat holds back to make room. A simple synth bass line repeats under a four-on-the-floor drum machine, with the snare on two and four and a closed hi-hat ticking along. Sustained synth pad chords sit underneath, and a high synth phrase loops on top. The tempo is moderate, and the groove is steady enough to dance to without pushing you. The room is dry and the mix is clean, which keeps Amaarae's breathy, clear voice close. The delivery slides between melody and something near speech, rhythmic and unhurried.

Critics split on it. African Folder heard SPINALL pledging himself to the alté scene, and iMullar called Amaarae's turn one of the album's highlights. Afrocritik thought the sparse backing didn't quite meet Amaarae's sound. That spareness is real, and it's also why the voice lands so close to you. In two minutes the song is gone, with nothing wasted.

It sticks because the hook lets you be the throne and the one kneeling at the same time, and asking to be undone turns out to be its own kind of power.
